The '''1740 [[FLLA]] World Cup''' was the 18th edition of the [[FLLA World Cup]], the quadrennial international [[Arraby]] tournament contested by the senior men's national teams of the member associations of the [[FLLA]]. It was held in [[Seytinemas]] across [[Mahea]] from 4 June to 2 July 1740, and was won by [[New Misos]], who defeated [[Lycroa]] 2–1 in the final at the Vulna Olympic Stadium in the host capital of [[Vulna]] to claim their first FLLA World Cup title. Thirty-two nations qualified for the final tournament, drawn from the seven continental confederations of the [[FLLA]], and contested 64 matches across seven host venues.

The 1740 edition was the first FLLA World Cup to be held in [[Mahea]] and the first to be contested by the present field of thirty-two teams. The expansion to a 32-team finals tournament was approved by the [[FLLA]] Council on 12 October 1737 under resolution 1737/8, and was accompanied by the introduction of a four-pot seeded draw and a standardised group-stage format that have since remained substantially unchanged. The 1740 final, contested between [[New Misos]] and [[Lycroa]] at the Vulna Olympic Stadium on 2 July, was the first FLLA World Cup match to be broadcast by a transcontinental radio relay, drawing an estimated half a million listeners across all seven continents of [[Andah]] in addition to the 63,400 spectators present at the ground.

The 1740 tournament is also remembered as the edition at which the FLLA's '''two-trophy system''' was inaugurated. Under FLLA Council resolution 1739/4, the rotating [[FLLA World Cup#The Andah Cup|Andah Cup]], a 38-centimetre silver-and-gold sculpture designed two years earlier by [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] sculptor Mariosa Calvelli, was presented for the first time alongside a bespoke permanent trophy commissioned by the host association. The Seytinemasi Arraby Federation's permanent trophy, '''The Vulna''', was retained in perpetuity by the winning [[New Misos|New Misosan]] association and is displayed at the Lunava Federal Museum in [[Lunava]]; the [[Andah Cup]] returned to FLLA headquarters in [[Tirna]] in the spring of 1741 for re-presentation at the [[1744 FLLA World Cup|1744 edition]] in [[Lycroa]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1739/resolution-1739-4|title=FLLA Council resolution 1739/4: establishment of the two-trophy system|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=4 November 1739}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/trophies/andah-cup|title=The Andah Cup: history, design and custodianship|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=24 June 1740}}</ref>

The competition is remembered as one of the most tactically cautious in the FLLA World Cup's history. A total of 147 goals were scored across the 64 matches at an average of 2.30 per match, the lowest goal-per-match average then recorded at any edition of the tournament. Five of the fifteen knockout-stage ties were decided by [[wikipedia:Penalty shoot-out (association football)|penalty shoot-out]] and a sixth by extra time. The most widely cited surprise of the competition was the run of the [[ACFVL]] qualifier [[Sattle]], a side ranked 117th in the pre-tournament [[FLLA]] standings, who eliminated the [[ATFVL]] winners [[Raledria]] on penalties in the round of sixteen and reached the quarter-finals, the deepest run by an Acrolan nation in the competition's history to that point.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1740/tournament-summary|title=Summary report of the 1740 FLLA World Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=14 August 1740}}</ref>

==Host selection==
{{Main|1740 FLLA World Cup bids}}

The bidding process for the 1740 FLLA World Cup was conducted in the pre-rotation framework that governed the competition between [[1700 FLLA World Cup|1700]] and the adoption of the [[FLLA World Cup#Expansion to 32 teams and the rotation policy (1740 to present)|confederation rotation policy]] in February 1740. Although the rotation policy was adopted by the FLLA Council on 4 February 1740, only four months before the opening match of the 1740 tournament, it applied only to the subsequent 1744 hosting cycle and to all editions thereafter, and did not affect the 1740 host selection, which had been confirmed by the FLLA Council under the older informal framework in October 1737. Under the informal practice then in force, hosting rights alternated between Ayuman and non-Ayuman bidders without a binding sequence; the FLLA Council retained an open invitation for candidate associations from all seven confederations to lodge expressions of interest, with the final decision taken by simple majority vote of the Council on the basis of a technical assessment by the FLLA Secretariat.

The Council opened the formal bidding window for the 1740 edition on 5 March 1736, two years before the customary host-confirmation date. Five candidate associations lodged formal bids ahead of the deadline of 30 June 1737: [[Seytinemas]] (representing the [[MAFVL]]), [[Etirha]] (representing the [[ATFVL]]), [[Verusa]] (representing the [[AYFVL]] as a back-up candidate to the recently confirmed [[1736 FLLA World Cup]] hosts), [[Quidic]] (representing the [[QUFVL]]) and [[Sanagara]] (representing the [[MSFVL]]). The [[Seytinemas|Seytinemasi]] bid, formally submitted by the Seytinemasi Arraby Federation in May 1737 under the personal patronage of the Vulna federal authorities, prevailed at the FLLA Council meeting of 12 October 1737 by seventeen votes to nine, with two abstentions.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/news/1737/seytinemas-confirmed|title=Seytinemas confirmed as 1740 FLLA World Cup hosts|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=12 October 1737}}</ref>

The Seytinemasi bid was supported in the FLLA Secretariat's technical assessment by three principal arguments: the [[Seytinemas|Seytinemese]] government's pledge of {{lahn}}340&nbsp;million towards stadium construction and transport improvements across the seven proposed host cities, the broader Mahean federations' commitment to a coordinated continental development plan in advance of any prospective expansion of the finals, and the strategic case for staging the first FLLA World Cup on the [[Mahea|Mahean]] continent in the seventh decade of the FLLA's existence. The decision passed amid lobbying by the [[AYFVL]] secretariat in favour of a return to [[Ayuma]] under the informal rotation, an objection the FLLA Council noted but did not sustain.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/news/1737/bid-assessment|title=Technical assessment of the 1740 FLLA World Cup candidate bids|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=20 September 1737}}</ref>

The total infrastructure budget pledged at the bid stage by the Seytinemasi federal government and the participating municipal authorities was {{lahn}}340&nbsp;million, of which {{lahn}}220&nbsp;million was directed towards stadium construction and renovation, {{lahn}}80&nbsp;million towards transport upgrades across the seven host cities, and {{lahn}}40&nbsp;million towards operational expenditure on broadcasting infrastructure, security and the volunteer programme. The budget was the largest single-host commitment to that date and reflected the [[Seytinemas|Seytinemese]] government's strategic emphasis on the tournament as a showcase of the country's post-1732 republican reconstruction.

==Participating teams and officials==

===Qualification===
{{Main|1740 FLLA World Cup qualification}}

The 1740 qualification programme was the first conducted to the 32-team finals format. Places at the finals were allocated across the seven [[FLLA]] confederations on the basis of fixed shares confirmed by the [[FLLA]] Council in November 1737, with provision for the host association to qualify automatically as of right under the standing FLLA hosting regulations. The allocation distributed seven places to the [[AYFVL]], five to the [[MAFVL]] (including the host), five to the [[MSFVL]], four to the [[ATFVL]], three to the [[NAFVL]], four to the [[QUFVL]] and four to the [[ACFVL]]; the allocation was retained substantially unchanged at the [[1744 FLLA World Cup|1744 edition]] and at every subsequent edition until the marginal reweighting of 1756.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1737/berth-allocation-1740|title=Continental berth allocation for the 1740 FLLA World Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=14 November 1737}}</ref>

Each confederation administered its own qualifying competition. The qualifying tournaments are summarised below; full results are recorded on the individual confederation pages.

Four first-round groups of five followed by a final octagonal round-robin. Qualified teams:
* {{Flagicon|New Misos}} [[New Misos]]
* {{Flagicon|Raledria}} [[Raledria]]
* {{Flagicon|Etirha}} [[Etirha]]
* {{Flagicon|Genaire}} [[Genaire]]

==== [[AYFVL]] (Ayuma) 7 berths ====
Seven qualifying groups; group winners qualified directly. Qualified teams:
* {{Flagicon|Lycroa}} [[Lycroa]]
* {{Flagicon|Emara}} [[Emara]]
* {{Flagicon|Verusa}} [[Verusa]]
* {{Flagicon|Darewa}} [[Darewa]]
* {{Flagicon|Siana}} [[Siana]]
* {{Flagicon|Praesyu}} [[Praesyu]]
* {{Flagicon|Fermori}} [[Fermori]]

A single 23-team double round-robin league. Qualified teams:
* {{Flagicon|United Delet}} [[United Delet]]

Four first-round groups followed by two final round-robin groups. Qualified teams:

The qualifying programme produced two notable outcomes. The first was the qualification of [[Fermori]], whose declaration of full national independence on 1 January 1740 became effective only five months before the start of the finals; the Fermorian Arraby Federation's qualification through the [[AYFVL]] Group G on 18 December 1739 was the first major international honour secured by an independent Fermorian side.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.faf.fer/1739/qualification|title=Fermorian Arraby Federation: 1740 FLLA World Cup qualification record|publisher=Fermorian Arraby Federation|date=20 December 1739}}</ref> The second was the qualification of the [[MSFVL]] for five separate places at the finals for the first time under the new allocation, ending the historical underrepresentation of [[Massir]] at the competition.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.msfvl.org/1739/qualification-summary|title=MSFVL 1740 FLLA World Cup qualification summary|publisher=[[MSFVL]]|date=4 February 1740}}</ref>

===Final draw===
{{Main|1740 FLLA World Cup seeding}}

The final draw for the group stage was held at the Vulna National Theatre in [[Vulna]] on 18 December 1739, six months before the opening match. The 32 qualified teams were drawn into four pots of eight on the basis of their pre-tournament [[FLLA]] rankings, with the host [[Seytinemas]] and the seven highest-ranked sides placed in the seeded pot. The four-pot seeded draw procedure, formally adopted by the FLLA Council under resolution 1739/3 in September 1739, was the first such procedure used at an FLLA World Cup and was retained at every subsequent edition through to the seeding reform of 1751.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1739/draw-procedure|title=Procedures for the 1740 FLLA World Cup final draw|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=8 September 1739}}</ref>

The ceremony was conducted by FLLA general secretary Halver Onstead, with retired internationals from each of the seven confederations drawing the team names from the pots. The draw was broadcast live on the Seytinemasi National Radio and relayed by twelve partner broadcasters across [[Mahea]], [[Ayuma]] and [[Atirha]]; it was the first FLLA World Cup draw to receive any form of international broadcast distribution.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1739/draw-ceremony|title=Official record of the 1740 FLLA World Cup final draw|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=20 December 1739}}</ref>

===Officials===
{{Main|1740 FLLA World Cup officials}}

The FLLA Referees Committee appointed nineteen refereeing trios and four support pairs drawn from a combined pool of fifteen nations, the broadest international composition of any officiating panel at an FLLA World Cup to that date. Selections were announced in two tranches between June 1739 and February 1740 following an assessment programme at the [[1739 FLLA Continental Champions Cup]] and at senior friendlies organised across the seven Seytinemasi host cities. The opening match was refereed by Mavren Cestaro of [[Verusa]] ([[AYFVL]]); the final was officiated by Tahito Marennas of [[Wundry]] ([[QUFVL]]) in his first appointment to an FLLA World Cup final, having earlier been appointed to the round-of-sixteen tie between [[Astye]] and [[Emara]] on 22 June and the quarter-final between [[New Misos]] and [[Trian]] on 25 June. Marennas would go on to officiate his second FLLA World Cup final four years later at the [[1744 FLLA World Cup|1744 edition]] in [[Lycroa]], becoming the first referee to take charge of consecutive FLLA World Cup finals.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1740/officials-announced|title=Match officials confirmed for the 1740 FLLA World Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=22 February 1740}}</ref>

==Squads==
{{Main|1740 FLLA World Cup squads}}

Each participating squad consisted of 22 players, two of whom were required to be goalkeepers. The 22-player squad allocation was newly introduced at the 1740 edition under FLLA Council resolution 1739/5, an increase from the 20-player squads in force at the [[1736 FLLA World Cup|1736 edition]] reflecting the lengthier knockout schedule under the new format. A total of 704 players were registered for the tournament, of whom 64 were goalkeepers. Each participating national association was required to confirm its final squad with the FLLA no later than seven days before the opening match.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1739/resolution-1739-5|title=FLLA Council resolution 1739/5: squad allocation for the 1740 finals|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=12 November 1739}}</ref>

The oldest player at the tournament was [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] goalkeeper Renar Carestano, who was 36 years and 281 days old at the start of the competition; the youngest was [[Fermori|Fermorian]] forward Aldis Kervanis, who at 19 years and 102 days became the youngest player to feature in an FLLA World Cup knockout match when he scored from the run of play in his country's [[#Round of 16|round-of-sixteen]] fixture against [[Praesyu]] on 23 June. The mean age of registered players across the tournament was 27.6 years.

The [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] central midfielder Cario Velarzo, appearing at his third FLLA World Cup after representing his country at the [[1732 FLLA World Cup|1732]] and [[1736 FLLA World Cup|1736 editions]], anchored the Lycroan midfield throughout the [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] run to the final. Velarzo would go on to appear at the [[1744 FLLA World Cup|1744 edition]] in his fourth tournament, setting the all-tournament record for repeat appearances by a single player at the FLLA World Cup; he was honoured at the 1740 closing ceremony as one of the [[#Awards|tournament's outstanding individual performers]] but the formal individual awards programme had not then been established and no individual prize was conferred. The [[New Misos|New Misosan]] forward Veram Sokri, who would score the opening goal of the [[#Final|1740 final]] and a total of six goals across the seven-match [[New Misos|New Misosan]] run, was the leading individual goalscorer of the finals tournament for a champion side; the leading individual goalscorer overall was [[Dahe|Dahen]] forward Avash Marenta with seven goals across the [[Dahe|Dahen]] knockout campaign (twelve including qualification).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/records/1740-individual-records|title=FLLA World Cup individual records: 1740 edition|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=18 August 1740}}</ref>

==Venues==
{{Main|1740 FLLA World Cup venues}}

Seven stadiums in seven host cities were used in the final tournament, all located in [[Seytinemas]]. Four of the seven were newly built for the tournament or substantially redeveloped during the bidding period; the remaining three were existing top-flight Seytinemasi venues that received targeted upgrades to seating and broadcasting facilities under FLLA Council resolution 1737/12. The seven-venue programme established the precedent of a single-host stadium plan in the seven-to-twelve venue range that has been followed at every subsequent FLLA World Cup of the modern era.

The opening match was held at the Vulna Olympic Stadium in [[Vulna]], the largest venue at the tournament and the principal final venue. The final on 2 July was held at the same ground; the third-place playoff between [[Dahe]] and [[Fermori]] was held at the Stadion Lunmar in [[Lunmar]] the previous day. The two semi-finals were divided between the Tarvic National Stadium in [[Tarvic]] and the Mansek Coastal Ground in [[Mansek]].

===Venue profiles===

The '''Vulna Olympic Stadium''', in the host capital of [[Vulna]], was the largest venue at the tournament and the principal final venue. The 64,000-seat ground, designed by the Seytinemasi architectural studio Mestoria–Vahn and inaugurated by the head of state of [[Seytinemas]] on 4 April 1740, was constructed on the site of the older Vulna Civic Athletics Ground (closed 1738) on the southern bank of the [[Lanol]] River. The ground hosted the opening match on 4 June between the hosts [[Seytinemas]] and [[Praesyu]], one of the four [[#Quarter-finals|quarter-finals]] on 25 June, one [[#Round of 16|round-of-sixteen]] tie, eight group-stage fixtures and the [[#Final|final]] itself on 2 July; the final drew an attendance of 63,400, just below the stadium's listed capacity.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.saf.sey/venues/vulna-olympic-stadium|title=Vulna Olympic Stadium: design and inauguration|publisher=Seytinemasi Arraby Federation|date=4 April 1740}}</ref>

The '''Tarvic National Stadium''' in [[Tarvic]], the second-largest venue with a capacity of 52,000, was originally opened in 1721 and extensively redeveloped between 1737 and 1740 to bring it within FLLA capacity guidance for knockout-stage fixtures. The ground hosted the first of the two [[#Semi-finals|semi-finals]], between [[New Misos]] and [[Dahe]], on 28 June, one [[#Quarter-finals|quarter-final]] on 25 June, one [[#Round of 16|round-of-sixteen]] tie, and seven group-stage fixtures.

The '''Stadion Lunmar''' in [[Lunmar]], a 48,000-seat ground completed in 1735 as part of the Seytinemasi government's federal sports investment programme, hosted the [[#Third place playoff|third-place playoff]] between [[Dahe]] and [[Fermori]] on 1 July, one [[#Quarter-finals|quarter-final]], one [[#Round of 16|round-of-sixteen]] tie and seven group-stage fixtures. The '''Mansek Coastal Ground''' in [[Mansek]], a 44,000-seat venue purpose-built for the tournament on a reclaimed coastal site and inaugurated in February 1740, hosted the second [[#Semi-finals|semi-final]] between [[Lycroa]] and [[Fermori]], one [[#Round of 16|round-of-sixteen]] tie and seven group-stage fixtures.

The '''Merlan Federal Stadium''' in [[Merlan]], a 41,000-seat ground completed in 1738 as the home venue of the Merlan domestic-league club Merlan Federal, hosted one [[#Quarter-finals|quarter-final]] on 26 June, one [[#Round of 16|round-of-sixteen]] tie and eight group-stage fixtures. The remaining two venues, the Vurklo Civic Stadium in [[Vurklo]] and the Sovarek Sports Ground in [[Sovarek]], each staged one [[#Round of 16|round-of-sixteen]] tie and seven group-stage fixtures.

==Innovations==

The 1740 FLLA World Cup introduced a substantial number of regulatory and presentational changes, several of which became durable features of the modern competition. The tournament was the first FLLA World Cup contested by the present field of thirty-two teams under the expansion approved by the FLLA Council in October 1737, and the first held under a standardised group-stage format of eight groups of four with the top two finishers advancing to a sixteen-team [[wikipedia:Single-elimination tournament|single-elimination]] knockout. The eight-group, sixteen-knockout structure has been retained without amendment at every subsequent edition of the tournament.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1737/resolution-1737-8|title=FLLA Council resolution 1737/8: expansion of the FLLA World Cup to 32 teams|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=12 October 1737}}</ref>

The 1740 tournament was also the first FLLA World Cup at which the four-pot seeded draw procedure was used, replacing the partially regional and ad-hoc seeding arrangements employed at the [[1732 FLLA World Cup|1732]] and [[1736 FLLA World Cup|1736 editions]]. Adopted by the FLLA Council under resolution 1739/3, the four-pot procedure was retained at every subsequent FLLA World Cup until the seeding reform of 1751. The squad-size regulation was also amended at the 1740 edition under resolution 1739/5, increasing the maximum squad from 20 to 22 players and requiring the inclusion of at least two goalkeepers; the revised allocation has been retained substantially unchanged to the present day.

The most enduring innovation of the 1740 tournament was the inauguration of the '''two-trophy system''' under FLLA Council resolution 1739/4. The pre-1740 [[FLLA World Cup#The Ayuma Cup|Ayuma Cup]] had been returned to the FLLA in 1738 by then-holders [[Emara]] ahead of the new arrangement, ending the older one-trophy practice of permanent transfer to the winning nation at each edition. In its place the FLLA introduced the rotating [[FLLA World Cup#The Andah Cup|Andah Cup]], retained in trust by the FLLA between editions and presented to the winning nation at the closing ceremony of each final, paired with a bespoke permanent trophy newly commissioned for every edition and retained in perpetuity by the winning association. Both trophies have been presented together at every closing ceremony from the 1740 edition onwards.

A further presentational change at the 1740 tournament was the introduction of an official mascot, an anthropomorphic Seytinemasi river otter named '''Lanori''' (after the [[Lanol]] River that runs through the host capital). The mascot programme has been continued by every subsequent host federation; the introduction of a bespoke official match ball and an official theme song, both of which became standard features of the modern competition, similarly date from the 1740 edition.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/heritage/1740-innovations|title=Innovations of the 1740 FLLA World Cup: an FLLA heritage record|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=18 December 1764}}</ref>

==Format==

The 32 qualified teams were divided into eight groups of four for the group stage, drawn at the [[#Final draw|final draw]] on 18 December 1739. Each group operated on a single round-robin basis, with each team playing three matches; teams were awarded three points for a win, one for a draw and none for a defeat. The top two teams from each group advanced to the [[#Knockout stage|knockout stage]] while the bottom two were eliminated. Tiebreakers between teams level on points were applied in the following order: overall goal difference, overall goals scored, head-to-head record, fair-play points, and, if necessary, a drawing of lots by the FLLA Organising Committee.

In the knockout stage, fixtures were single-elimination ties played over 90 minutes; ties level at the end of normal time were extended by a single 30-minute period of [[wikipedia:Extra time|extra time]] of two 15-minute halves, with a [[wikipedia:Penalty shoot-out (association football)|penalty shoot-out]] used to decide ties that remained level after extra time. The two semi-final losers contested a [[#Third place playoff|third-place playoff]] on 1 July 1740, the day before the final.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1739/regulations-1740|title=Regulations of the 1740 FLLA World Cup: group-stage and knockout format|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=22 November 1739}}</ref>

==Opening ceremony==

The opening ceremony of the 1740 FLLA World Cup was held at the Vulna Olympic Stadium on 4 June 1740, ninety minutes before the kick-off of the opening match between the hosts [[Seytinemas]] and [[Praesyu]]. Directed by Seytinemasi stage producer Loren Vahnari and choreographed by Andrea Cestori, the ceremony lasted 28 minutes and featured 580 dancers, 140 musicians and a massed processional entrance representing each of the seven continental confederations of the [[FLLA]]. The performance opened with a sequence drawn from the [[Seytinemas|Seytinemese]] coronation rite of the [[Oum's dynasty]], performed under the dual ecclesiastical patronage of the [[Kallimethra|Doxis Kallimethran]] and [[Thessovai]] communities of [[Vulna]] in recognition of the host nation's mixed religious tradition. A processional sequence depicting the migration routes of the seven seafaring confederations across the globe of [[Andah]] followed, before transitioning to a closing tableau in which 32 children in the national colours of the participating nations took the field together at the centre circle.

Attending dignitaries included the head of state of [[Seytinemas]], the President of the FLLA Council Halver Onstead, the heads of state of [[Trian]], [[Chaenia]] and [[New Misos]], and 47 ambassadors and senior diplomatic representatives. The ceremony was broadcast live on radio by the Seytinemasi National Radio and relayed by 18 partner broadcasters across [[Mahea]], [[Ayuma]] and parts of [[Atirha]]; this was the first FLLA World Cup opening ceremony to be broadcast outside the host continent.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.snr.sey/1740/opening-ceremony|title=Opening ceremony of the 1740 FLLA World Cup: production notes and broadcast record|publisher=Seytinemasi National Radio|date=4 June 1740}}</ref>

==Group stage==

The 32 qualified teams were drawn into eight groups of four. Each group operated on a single round-robin basis, with each team playing three matches; the top two finishers in each group advanced to the [[#Knockout stage|knockout stage]] while the bottom two were eliminated. Group rankings were settled first on points (three for a win, one for a draw), then on goal difference and goals scored.

The group stage produced three perfect records: [[Praesyu]] in Group B, [[Astye]] in Group E and [[Raledria]] in Group H each took maximum points from their three matches. The host nation [[Seytinemas]] advanced in second place in Group B behind a [[Praesyu|Praesyuan]] side that conceded only a single goal across the group; the hosts secured progression with a 2–1 win over [[Isari]] on the final matchday at the Vulna Olympic Stadium. Two upsets in the group stage attracted particular comment. The first was the 1–2 defeat of the [[AYFVL]] qualifying winners [[Lycroa]] by the [[NAFVL]] qualifier [[Astye]] in Group E, recorded across a pre-tournament [[FLLA]]-ranking gap of 188 points; [[Lycroa]] recovered to advance as Group E runners-up on goal difference behind the unbeaten [[Astye]]. The second, of greater significance for the eventual shape of the knockout stage, was the 2–1 opening-matchday defeat of the [[AYFVL]] qualifier [[Siana]] by the 117th-ranked [[ACFVL]] qualifier [[Sattle]] at the Stadion Lunmar, the first leg of the [[Sattle|Sattlean]] side's progression to a runners-up finish in Group G and the deepest run by an [[Acrola|Acrolan]] side at any FLLA World Cup to that date.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1740/group-g-summary|title=Group G summary: Sattle progression and Siana elimination|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=14 June 1740}}</ref>

All times listed are Standard Seytinemasi Time ([[wikipedia:UTC+03:00|SST]], [[wikipedia:UTC|UTC]]+3).

==Knockout stage==

The knockout stage involved the sixteen teams that advanced from the group stage. Matches still level after 90 minutes were extended by a 30-minute period of [[wikipedia:Extra time|extra time]]; if scores remained tied after extra time, the tie was decided by [[wikipedia:Penalty shoot-out (association football)|penalty shoot-out]]. Five of the sixteen knockout-stage ties were decided by penalty shoot-out and a sixth (the third-place playoff) by extra time, the highest combined total of penalty and extra-time deciders recorded at any FLLA World Cup. The cumulative goal total across the sixteen knockout matches was 35, an average of 2.19 per match, slightly below the tournament average of 2.30.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1740/knockout-statistical-summary|title=Statistical summary of the 1740 FLLA World Cup knockout stage|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=12 July 1740}}</ref>

===Round of 16===

The eight group winners were drawn against the eight group runners-up, with each match-up pairing teams from different groups. Three of the eight ties were decided by penalty shoot-out, the highest single-round total of shoot-out finishes in FLLA World Cup history to that date, and a fourth was won by a single goal. The most widely publicised result of the round was the 1–1 (3–4 pen.) defeat of the unbeaten [[ATFVL]] qualifying winners [[Raledria]] by the 117th-ranked [[ACFVL]] qualifier [[Sattle]] at the Vulna Olympic Stadium on 24 June. The result, recorded across a pre-tournament [[FLLA]]-ranking gap of 491 points, was the most significant upset by ranking margin in the modern history of the competition at the time and remained an unbroken record until equalled at the [[1764 FLLA World Cup|1764 edition]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/records/upsets-ranking|title=FLLA World Cup upsets by ranking margin: the Sattle–Raledria record|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=25 June 1740}}</ref> The host nation [[Seytinemas]], who had advanced from Group B as runners-up to [[Praesyu]], were eliminated by the [[ATFVL]] qualifying winners [[New Misos]] 1–2 at the Vulna Olympic Stadium on the opening day of the knockout stage.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.snr.sey/sport/1740/host-elimination|title=Host elimination: New Misos defeat Seytinemas at the Vulna Olympic Stadium|publisher=Seytinemasi National Radio|date=21 June 1740}}</ref>

===Quarter-finals===

The four quarter-finals produced two ties decided in normal time and two on penalties. [[New Misos]] beat [[Trian]] 2–0 at the Vulna Olympic Stadium through two first-half goals by forward Veram Sokri, his third and fourth strikes of the tournament; the result took [[New Misos]] to the semi-finals for the first time since the [[1716 FLLA World Cup|1716 edition]]. [[Dahe]] beat [[Emara]] 2–1 at the Tarvic National Stadium, with forward Avash Marenta scoring both [[Dahe|Dahen]] goals in a result that became the [[ATFVL]] qualifying winners' [[Emara|Emaran]] elimination at the first knockout opportunity. [[Fermori]] beat [[United Delet]] 6–5 on penalties after a goalless 120 minutes at the Stadion Lunmar in the longest shoot-out of the tournament, with [[Fermori|Fermorian]] captain Aldis Kervanis converting the decisive sixth kick. [[Lycroa]] beat the giant-killers [[Sattle]] 3–2 on penalties after a goalless 120 minutes at the Merlan Federal Stadium, with [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] goalkeeper Renar Carestano saving the second and fourth [[Sattle|Sattlean]] kicks to end the [[ACFVL]] qualifier's run.

===Semi-finals===

The first semi-final at the Tarvic National Stadium was contested between the [[ATFVL]] qualifying winners [[New Misos]] and the [[MSFVL]] qualifier [[Dahe]], the latter making their first appearance in an FLLA World Cup semi-final. [[Dahe]] opened the scoring through forward Avash Marenta in the 29th minute, riding a back line marshalled by captain Bhairav Tashain that the FLLA Tactical Review Committee later described as the most cohesive [[Massir|Massiran]] defensive unit in modern competition. [[New Misos]] equalised through forward Veram Sokri in the 58th minute and took the lead 11 minutes from time through the [[New Misos|New Misosan]] captain Verras Tonelka, whose long-range strike from outside the penalty area survived a review by the line judge to settle the tie. The result took [[New Misos]] to a first FLLA World Cup final, ending [[Dahe]]'s best run at the competition to that point.

The second semi-final at the Mansek Coastal Ground was decided inside 90 minutes by two second-half goals from [[Lycroa]]. The match between [[Lycroa]] and the newly independent [[Fermori]] had been cautiously contested through a goalless first half before [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] midfielder Cario Velarzo broke the deadlock in the 54th minute from a low cross by right-back Marec Toranci, with forward Mario Calvenza adding a second 22 minutes from time. The result took [[Lycroa]] to the FLLA World Cup final for the third time in their history and the first since their 0–0 victory at the [[1680 FLLA World Cup|1680 edition]] (decided by coin toss), and eliminated the [[Fermori|Fermorian]] side at the deepest point of any national side fewer than six months removed from independence in FLLA history.

===Third place playoff===

The third-place playoff was contested between the two losing semi-finalists at the Stadion Lunmar on 1 July, the day before the [[#Final|final]]. [[Dahe]] beat [[Fermori]] 2–1 after extra time to take third place at the tournament, with forward Avash Marenta scoring both [[Dahe|Dahen]] goals to extend his all-tournament tally to twelve and become the leading individual scorer at the competition. [[Fermori]]'s consolation goal was scored by the 19-year-old forward Aldis Kervanis from a low cross by Lestor Renvad in the 78th minute. The result gave [[Dahe]] their highest finish at an FLLA World Cup in the competition's history and produced the only extra-time decision in the knockout stage outside of the four penalty shoot-out finishes.

===Final===
{{Main|1740 FLLA World Cup final}}

The final was contested between the [[ATFVL]] qualifying winners [[New Misos]] and the [[AYFVL]] qualifier [[Lycroa]] on 2 July 1740 at the Vulna Olympic Stadium in [[Vulna]] in front of an attendance of 63,400. [[New Misos]] entered the match having scored seven goals across their five previous fixtures, while [[Lycroa]] had reached the final having conceded only two goals in their five matches. The match was contested in front of a global radio audience estimated at half a million individuals across the seven continents of [[Andah]], the first FLLA World Cup match to be broadcast outside its host continent in real time.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1740/final-report|title=Match report: 1740 FLLA World Cup final, New Misos 2–1 Lycroa|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=3 July 1740}}</ref>

[[New Misos]] took the lead in the 19th minute through forward Veram Sokri, who slid in unmarked at the back post to convert a low cross by captain Verras Tonelka after a quickly worked free kick on the right wing. [[Lycroa]] equalised seven minutes before half time through forward Mario Calvenza, who turned in a rebound off the inside of the post after [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] midfielder Cario Velarzo had struck the woodwork from outside the penalty area; the equalising goal levelled the match at 1–1 at half time. The second half remained tightly contested through both periods of normal time until forward Renri Voltaska of [[New Misos]] scored the winner in the 71st minute, sweeping in from close range after [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] goalkeeper Renar Carestano had parried a long-range effort from Tonelka into the path of the onrushing Voltaska. [[Lycroa]] pressed for an equaliser through the final fifteen minutes without registering a clear chance against the [[New Misos|New Misosan]] goalkeeper Olen Karlamir, and the match concluded with a 2–1 victory to [[New Misos]] and the first FLLA World Cup title in the country's history.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.snr.sey/sport/1740/final|title=New Misos win first world title at Vulna Olympic Stadium|publisher=Seytinemasi National Radio|date=2 July 1740}}</ref>

The win gave [[New Misos]] their first FLLA World Cup title; the side would defend the crown unsuccessfully at the [[1744 FLLA World Cup|1744 edition]] in [[Lycroa]], reaching the semi-final stage before elimination by the eventual runners-up [[Easuhura]], and would secure their second title four years later at the [[1748 FLLA World Cup|1748 edition]] on home soil. [[Lycroa]] would return to the final at the following edition as host nation and secure their fifth FLLA World Cup title in a 0–0 (3–0 pens) win over [[Easuhura]], the final's outcome widely framed in the [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] press as a redemption result for the generation defeated at the Vulna Olympic Stadium four years earlier.

==Statistics==

===Goalscoring===

[[Dahe]] finished as the tournament's leading goalscoring nation with 14 goals across seven matches, ahead of second-placed [[New Misos]] (12 in seven) and joint second [[United Delet]] (12 in four). The overall goal-per-match average of 2.30 across the 64 matches of the tournament was the lowest at any FLLA World Cup recorded to that date, and remained an unbroken record at any subsequent edition through to the time of writing. The FLLA Tactical Review Committee, which would be formally constituted ahead of the [[1744 FLLA World Cup|1744 edition]] under FLLA Council resolution 1743/9 in part as a direct response to the scoring patterns of 1740, attributed the low average in its first retrospective assessment to the spread of compact rear-defensive systems among the leading sides and to the increasing standardisation of the offside trap as a defensive tactic at international level.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1740/scoring-review|title=Retrospective scoring review of the 1740 FLLA World Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=14 November 1744}}</ref>

The leading individual goalscorer at the tournament was [[Dahe|Dahen]] forward Avash Marenta with seven goals across the seven matches of [[Dahe]]'s run to third place (twelve in total including the qualifying campaign). The next most prolific individual scorer in the finals was [[New Misos|New Misosan]] forward Veram Sokri with six goals, all scored in the knockout stage and including a brace in the [[#Round of 16|round of sixteen]] against the hosts [[Seytinemas]], a brace in the [[#Quarter-finals|quarter-final]] against [[Trian]], and the opening goal of the [[#Final|final]] itself.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1740/individual-goalscoring|title=Individual goalscoring at the 1740 FLLA World Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=12 July 1740}}</ref>

===Discipline===

The FLLA Disciplinary Committee issued a total of 158 yellow cards and 7 red cards across the 64 matches of the tournament, an average of 2.47 yellows and 0.11 reds per match. The most-cautioned team across the tournament was [[Acetoa]], with 11 yellow cards and 1 red across their four matches; [[Praesyu]] received the fewest among the participating teams, with two yellows and no reds across their four matches. Two players received red cards in the knockout stage, one each at the round-of-sixteen and quarter-final stages.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/discipline/1740-summary|title=FLLA Disciplinary Committee: 1740 FLLA World Cup disciplinary summary|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=18 July 1740}}</ref>

==Awards==

The formal individual awards programme of the modern FLLA World Cup was not yet in place at the 1740 edition. Of the awards subsequently presented at every edition since the [[1744 FLLA World Cup|1744 tournament]] (the FLLA Vairan Ball, the FLLA Marskval and the FLLA Bastion), none had been formally constituted under FLLA Council resolution by the closing ceremony at the Vulna Olympic Stadium on 2 July 1740. The 1740 tournament marked the formal recognition only of the '''leading goalscoring nation''' under FLLA Council resolution 1739/4, the same instrument that introduced the two-trophy system; the prize was presented to the [[Dahe|Dahen]] Arraby Federation at the closing ceremony alongside the [[#Trophies|Andah Cup]] presentation to the [[New Misos|New Misosan]] champions.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1740/awards-record|title=Awards record of the 1740 FLLA World Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=4 July 1740}}</ref>

A precursor to the modern '''FLLA Vairan Ball''' was conferred at the 1740 closing ceremony by an informal panel of seven [[Mahea|Mahean]] sports journalists convened by the Seytinemasi Arraby Federation in advance of the final. The journalists' panel selected the [[New Misos|New Misosan]] captain and central midfielder Verras Tonelka as the most outstanding individual performer at the tournament, citing his contribution to the seven-match unbeaten run of the eventual champions and his decisive long-range strike in the [[#Semi-finals|semi-final]] against [[Dahe]]. The selection was not recognised under any formal FLLA regulation in force at the time and was distinguished by the FLLA Council in 1743 from the standardised FLLA Vairan Ball programme adopted ahead of the [[1744 FLLA World Cup|1744 edition]] under FLLA Council resolution 1743/4. Tonelka's recognition is recorded in subsequent FLLA literature as the first ''informal'' Vairan Ball; the [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] midfielder Cario Velarzo, recipient of the formal award four years later at the [[1744 FLLA World Cup|1744 edition]], was named alongside Tonelka in the 1740 panel's published list of three nominees.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1744/golden-ball-history|title=History of the FLLA Vairan Ball: precursor selections at the 1740 edition|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=8 July 1744}}</ref>

==Preparations and costs==

The total budget allocated to the 1740 FLLA World Cup by the Seytinemasi Arraby Federation and the federal government of [[Seytinemas]] was {{lahn}}340&nbsp;million. Of this, {{lahn}}220&nbsp;million was directed towards stadium construction and renovation across the seven venues, {{lahn}}80&nbsp;million towards transport upgrades (principally the [[Vulna]]–[[Tarvic]] coastal rail corridor and arterial road improvements connecting the seven host cities), and {{lahn}}40&nbsp;million towards operational expenditure including security, broadcasting infrastructure and the volunteer programme. The budget was the largest single-host commitment recorded by any FLLA World Cup to that date and reflected the [[Seytinemas|Seytinemese]] government's emphasis on the tournament as a showcase of the country's post-1732 republican reconstruction.

Four of the seven venues, comprising the Vulna Olympic Stadium, the Mansek Coastal Ground, the Merlan Federal Stadium and the Stadion Lunmar, were either newly built or extensively redeveloped for the tournament. The newest, the Mansek Coastal Ground, was inaugurated on 18 February 1740, less than four months before the opening match; the Vulna Olympic Stadium was inaugurated on 4 April 1740. Total stadium construction overran the original budget by approximately 11&nbsp;per&nbsp;cent, principally because of cost escalation at the Vulna Olympic Stadium and the foundation works at the Mansek Coastal Ground; the federal government absorbed the overrun under a guarantee provision agreed with the Seytinemasi Arraby Federation at the bid stage in November 1737.

The combined security operation involved 12,500 police and military personnel deployed across the seven host cities, the largest such single-nation deployment in the competition's history at the time. No serious incidents were reported during the competition. Total tournament revenue, audited by the FLLA in September 1740, was {{lahn}}460&nbsp;million, against costs of {{lahn}}340&nbsp;million, yielding a net surplus of {{lahn}}120&nbsp;million. Under the FLLA's standard host-association allocation then in force, {{lahn}}55&nbsp;million was returned to the Seytinemasi Arraby Federation, with the remainder retained by the FLLA for general administrative purposes and worldwide development programmes.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/audit/1740-final-accounts|title=Audited final accounts of the 1740 FLLA World Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=8 September 1740}}</ref>

==Marketing==
{{Main|1740 FLLA World Cup marketing}}

The marketing programme for the 1740 FLLA World Cup was overseen by the Seytinemasi Arraby Federation in partnership with the FLLA's commercial division, with creative direction by the [[Vulna]]-based studio Mestoria–Vahn. The programme included the official emblem, mascot, match ball and theme song (see [[#Symbols|Symbols]] below), a domestic travelling-trophy tour that visited 14 cities across [[Seytinemas]] in the year preceding the tournament, and a two-tier sponsorship structure of three worldwide partners and seven host-nation partners. Total sponsorship revenue was {{lahn}}90&nbsp;million, the first commercial sponsorship programme to exceed [[lahn|{{lahn}}]]50&nbsp;million at any FLLA World Cup and the foundation of the tiered sponsorship structure adopted at every subsequent edition.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/commercial/1740-sponsorship|title=1740 FLLA World Cup commercial and sponsorship summary|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=22 August 1740}}</ref>

==Symbols==
{{Main|1740 FLLA World Cup symbols}}

===Emblem===

The official emblem of the tournament, designed by the [[Vulna]]-based studio Mestoria–Vahn and unveiled at the Vulna National Theatre on 2 June 1739, depicts a stylised representation of the globe of [[Andah]] supported by two abstracted figures drawn from the same iconographic register as the rotating [[FLLA World Cup#The Andah Cup|Andah Cup]], framed by a wave motif borrowed from the heraldry of the [[Lanol]] River basin. The radial framing was intended to evoke both the host nation's [[Mahea|Mahean]] coastal geography and the global reach of the expanded 32-team competition. The emblem received the FLLA Council's formal endorsement in November 1739 after a four-week consultation period with the seven confederations.

===Mascot===

The official mascot of the 1740 FLLA World Cup, named '''Lanori''', is an anthropomorphic [[Lanol]] River otter dressed in the red-and-gold national colours of [[Seytinemas]]. The mascot was selected by the Seytinemasi Arraby Federation in March 1739 from a shortlist of six candidate designs developed by the [[Vulna]]-based studio Mestoria–Vahn, with the final selection ratified by the host federation's mascot committee in a private ballot. The 1740 edition was the first FLLA World Cup at which an official mascot was deployed; subsequent editions have adopted a public-vote selection model under FLLA Council resolution 1743/12, but the 1740 mascot is recognised in subsequent FLLA literature as the foundational reference for the modern mascot programme.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1739/mascot-history|title=Lanori: the first official mascot of the FLLA World Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=22 March 1739}}</ref>

===Match ball===

The official match ball, manufactured by the [[Vulna]]-based sports equipment maker Tonari Sport, was branded the '''Lanara'''. The Lanara featured a hand-stitched 32-panel construction in a cream-and-gold livery; it was the first bespoke FLLA World Cup match ball, replacing the older practice of using a leading domestic-league ball drawn from the host association. The 32-panel hand-stitched construction was retained at every FLLA World Cup through to the [[1752 FLLA World Cup|1752 edition]] before its replacement by the thermally-bonded design of the 1756 ball.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.tonarisport.sey/products/lanara-1740|title=The Lanara: official match ball of the 1740 FLLA World Cup|publisher=Tonari Sport|date=14 February 1740}}</ref>

===Permanent trophy===

The permanent trophy of the 1740 FLLA World Cup, presented to the winners alongside the rotating [[FLLA World Cup#The Andah Cup|Andah Cup]] at the closing ceremony of the final, was '''The Vulna''', a 42-centimetre gilded silver sculpture commissioned by the Seytinemasi Arraby Federation from the [[Vulna]]-based atelier Mestoria–Vahn. The work depicts a stylised river otter supporting a representation of the globe of [[Andah]], a motif intended to recall both the host capital's riverine character and the mascot Lanori developed by the same atelier. The trophy was unveiled at the Vulna National Theatre on 4 April 1740 alongside the inauguration of the Vulna Olympic Stadium. Following the [[#Final|2–1 win]] by [[New Misos]] over [[Lycroa]], The Vulna was transferred to permanent retention by the [[New Misos|New Misosan]] association and is displayed at the Lunava Federal Museum in [[Lunava]], where it has remained since the closing ceremony of the tournament on 2 July 1740.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1740/permanent-trophy|title=The Vulna: 1740 FLLA World Cup permanent trophy|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=4 April 1740}}</ref>

===Theme song===

The official theme song of the tournament, "Marsia Lanori" ("Anthem of the Otter"), was composed by Seytinemasi musician Tomian Vahnari with lyrics jointly written by Vahnari and the vocalist Liaria Cestori, who also performed the track. The studio recording was released on 4 April 1740, the same day as the inauguration of the Vulna Olympic Stadium, and topped the Seytinemasi domestic music charts across April and May 1740. "Marsia Lanori" is the first official FLLA World Cup theme song and the foundational reference for the tournament-theme tradition continued at every subsequent edition.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.snr.sey/charts/1740-may|title=Seytinemasi domestic chart summary, May 1740|publisher=Seytinemasi National Radio|date=2 June 1740}}</ref>

==Media==
{{Main|1740 FLLA World Cup broadcasting rights}}

The 1740 FLLA World Cup was broadcast in 41 countries by 17 official radio partners, the broadest cumulative international broadcasting reach of any FLLA World Cup to that date. Domestic broadcasting rights in [[Seytinemas]] were held by Seytinemasi National Radio (SNR), which produced the host radio feed and broadcast all 64 matches across its terrestrial radio network. The international rights for the [[AYFVL]] region were held by the [[Verusa|Verusan]] public-service broadcaster VRT; the [[ATFVL]] rights by the [[New Misos|New Misosan]] National Network (NMNN); and the [[MSFVL]] rights by a two-broadcaster consortium led by the Dahen National Radio.

The most widely cited innovation of the 1740 broadcasting programme was the '''transcontinental radio relay''' organised for the final on 2 July, the first FLLA World Cup match to be carried in real time outside its host continent. The relay arrangement, agreed in principle at a broadcasting summit convened by the FLLA in March 1740 and ratified by 23 partner associations across [[Mahea]], [[Ayuma]], [[Atirha]], [[New Ayre]], [[Massir]], [[Quia]] and [[Acrola]] in May 1740, allowed the [[#Final|final]] to be heard in real time on every continent of [[Andah]]; the FLLA reported a cumulative live audience for the match of approximately 500,000 individual listeners in addition to the 63,400 spectators at the Vulna Olympic Stadium. The success of the 1740 relay arrangement was retained and extended at every subsequent FLLA World Cup, and is widely regarded in subsequent FLLA literature as the foundational moment of the modern globally broadcast FLLA World Cup.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1740/transcontinental-relay|title=The transcontinental relay of the 1740 FLLA World Cup final|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=2 July 1740}}</ref>

===Attendance===

Cumulative attendance across the 64 matches of the tournament was 2,048,000 spectators, an average of 32,000 per match. The highest single-match attendance was the 63,400 recorded at the [[#Final|final]] between [[New Misos]] and [[Lycroa]] at the Vulna Olympic Stadium, just below the stadium's listed all-seater capacity of 64,000; the lowest was the 24,800 attending the Group F fixture between [[Haiza]] and [[Candenat]] at the Tarvic National Stadium on 13 June. The three highest single-match attendances of the tournament were all recorded at the Vulna Olympic Stadium, with the [[#Final|final]], the [[#Round of 16|round-of-sixteen]] tie between the hosts [[Seytinemas]] and [[New Misos]], and the [[#Quarter-finals|quarter-final]] between [[New Misos]] and [[Trian]] all drawing crowds in excess of 60,000.

==Controversies==

The most prominent dispute of the tournament arose from the Group E fixture between the [[AYFVL]] qualifying winners [[Lycroa]] and the [[NAFVL]] qualifier [[Astye]] at the Mansek Coastal Ground on 6 June, in which [[Lycroa]] were defeated 1–2 in what was recorded across a pre-tournament [[FLLA]]-ranking gap of 188 points. The [[AYFVL]] secretariat lodged an informal protest with the FLLA Refereeing Committee on 8 June, contending that a second-half goal by [[Astye]] had been allowed to stand despite an apparent foul by the [[Astye|Astyan]] forward Tarcan in the build-up. The FLLA Refereeing Committee declined to entertain the protest on 9 June, citing the finality of on-field decisions under the laws of the game then in force, and the result was undisturbed.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/referees/1740/ayfvl-protest|title=FLLA Refereeing Committee decision on the AYFVL protest of 8 June 1740|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=9 June 1740}}</ref>

A second incident, the dismissal of [[Sattle|Sattlean]] central defender Renze Kebahari in the 109th minute of the [[#Round of 16|round-of-sixteen]] tie against [[Raledria]] for a second bookable offence, was widely cited at the time as a notable refereeing call: the second yellow card was issued for an apparent dissent gesture rather than a foul, and the [[Sattle|Sattlean]] Arraby Federation later contended that the dismissal had been disproportionate to the offence given the stage of the tie. The FLLA Refereeing Committee declined to entertain the [[Sattle|Sattlean]] complaint on 28 June, again citing the finality of on-field decisions under the laws of the game; Kebahari was suspended from the [[#Quarter-finals|quarter-final]] against [[Lycroa]] and the [[Sattle|Sattlean]] side were eliminated at the close of that fixture.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/referees/1740/kebahari-decision|title=FLLA Refereeing Committee decision on the Kebahari dismissal|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=28 June 1740}}</ref>

A third dispute, of an administrative character, arose from the relayed broadcasting arrangements of the [[#Final|final]] itself: a small number of partner associations in the [[Quia|Quian]] confederation reported transmission interruptions of between four and seventeen minutes in length during the second half, attributed in a subsequent FLLA broadcasting review to an atmospheric disturbance affecting one of the four overland relay links. The FLLA Council's broadcasting committee published a clarification of the relay protocol in November 1740 in response, and the relay specifications adopted at the [[1744 FLLA World Cup|1744 edition]] included redundant overland link provisioning that became standard practice from that edition onwards.

==Aftermath==

[[New Misos]]'s victory was the first FLLA World Cup title secured by an [[ATFVL]] association since the [[1716 FLLA World Cup|1716 edition]] (a 2–1 win for [[Raledria]] in [[Easuhura]]) and the first by an [[ATFVL]] member other than [[Raledria]] in the worldwide format of the competition, [[Raledria]] having accounted for each of the three [[ATFVL]] titles secured at the [[1700 FLLA World Cup|1700]], [[1712 FLLA World Cup|1712]] and [[1716 FLLA World Cup|1716]] editions.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/records/atfvl-titles|title=ATFVL FLLA World Cup titles: historical record|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=14 July 1740}}</ref> The result was widely celebrated across [[New Misos]], where the team's homecoming parade through central [[Lunava]] on 7 July 1740 drew an estimated crowd of 1.3 million along a five-kilometre route from the city's principal square to the Lunava Federal Museum, the institution to which the permanent trophy [[#Permanent trophy|The Vulna]] was subsequently transferred for permanent display.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nmnn.mis/news/1740/homecoming-parade|title=New Misos homecoming: 1.3 million line Lunava streets|publisher=New Misosan National Network|date=7 July 1740}}</ref>

Across [[Seytinemas]], the tournament was widely judged a substantial organisational success. An independent post-event report commissioned by the Seytinemasi federal government and published in October 1740 estimated the net economic contribution to the host economy at {{lahn}}820&nbsp;million, against gross public expenditure of {{lahn}}340&nbsp;million across infrastructure and operations. International visitor arrivals across [[Seytinemas]] over the tournament period totalled 285,000, the highest cumulative tournament-period visitor figure recorded in [[Mahea]] up to that date. The Vulna Olympic Stadium, the Mansek Coastal Ground and the Stadion Lunmar were retained as permanent national and federal venues following the closing ceremony, and the matchday public transport provision introduced for the tournament was retained as a permanent matchday provision in [[Vulna]] and [[Tarvic]] by subsequent municipal decisions.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.gov.sey/1740/post-event-report|title=1740 FLLA World Cup post-event economic impact report|publisher=Seytinemasi Federal Government|date=18 October 1740}}</ref>

The unusually low overall scoring at the tournament, with a goal-per-match average of 2.30 across the 64 fixtures, prompted the FLLA Council's first formal review of in-play tactical trends and contributed to the constitution of the standing FLLA Tactical Review Committee at the [[1744 FLLA World Cup|1744 edition]] under FLLA Council resolution 1743/9. The Committee's later retrospective assessment of the 1740 tournament identified the spread of compact rear-defensive systems and the increasing standardisation of the offside trap as the principal drivers of the low scoring, findings that informed the procedural amendments to the laws of the game adopted by the [[FLLA]] in 1746.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/tactical-review/1740-retrospective|title=Retrospective tactical review of the 1740 FLLA World Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=14 November 1744}}</ref>

The next edition of the FLLA World Cup, the [[1744 FLLA World Cup]], was awarded to a single-nation [[AYFVL]] bid from [[Lycroa]] at the FLLA Council meeting of 18 March 1741, returning the tournament to [[Ayuma]] under the new confederation rotation framework adopted in February 1740. The Lycroan candidacy was framed throughout the bidding process as a national showcase of the recently reunified Federal Republic of Lycroa, formed on the completion of the [[Lycroan reunification]] in September 1738. The 1744 final between the host nation [[Lycroa]] and [[Easuhura]] was widely framed in advance as both a redemption fixture for the [[Lycroa|Lycroan]] generation defeated at the Vulna Olympic Stadium in the 1740 final and as the closing showpiece of [[Lycroa|Lycroa's]] first quadrennial cycle as a unified state; [[Lycroa]] would lift their fifth FLLA World Cup title at the [[1744 FLLA World Cup|1744 edition]] after a 0–0 (3–0 pens) win over [[Easuhura]] at the Estadio Huifarn.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/news/1741/1744-host-confirmation|title=Lycroa confirmed as 1744 FLLA World Cup hosts under the confederation rotation framework|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=18 March 1741}}</ref>
